summary.text: Writing \(D\) for decimal digit sum, the proof establishes the nine’s-complement identities \(D(x)+D(10^k-1-x)=9k\) and \(D(5x)+D(5(10^k-1-x))=9k\), with the latter reduced digitwise to \(\lfloor r/2\rfloor+5(r\bmod 2)+\lfloor(9-r)/2\rfloor+5((9-r)\bmod 2)=9\). Hence the sign contributions at \(x\) and \(10^k-1-x\) are opposites, so the terms between the two symmetric cumulative indices pair off and cancel.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(n)=\text{the sum of the decimal digits of }n,
\]
with \(D(0)=0\), and put
\[
\varepsilon(n)=\operatorname{sign}(D(5n)-D(n))\in\{-1,0,1\}.
\]
Thus, if
\[
F(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\varepsilon(j),
\]
then the sequence in the statement is \(a(n)=F(n)\) (or, in the given natural-number presentation, the natural-number image of this integer sum). We will prove that the two relevant integer sums \(F(n)\) are equal; applying the natural-number conversion therefore preserves the equality.

We first establish the decimal digit-sum identities needed for the reflection argument.

For every \(A\ge 0\) and every digit \(0\le B<10\),
\[
D(10A+B)=D(A)+B. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, \(B\) is the units digit of \(10A+B\), and the remaining decimal digits are exactly those of \(A\). Equivalently, for arbitrary \(n\),
\[
D(n)=n\bmod 10+D(\lfloor n/10\rfloor). \tag{2}
\]
These formulas also hold when the number involved is zero.

We need a slightly more specialized formula concerning multiplication by \(5\). For every \(q\ge 0\), division by \(2\) gives
\[
5q=10\left\lfloor\frac q2\right\rfloor+5(q\bmod 2). \tag{3}
\]
The last term is either \(0\) or \(5\), so by (1),
\[
D(5q)=D\left(\left\lfloor\frac q2\right\rfloor\right)+5(q\bmod 2). \tag{4}
\]
More generally, if \(0\le c<5\), then adding \(c\) to \(5q\) causes no carry from the units digit, because that units digit is either \(0\) or \(5\). Consequently,
\[
D(5q+c)=D(5q)+c. \tag{5}
\]

Now let \(0\le r<10\). Since
\[
5(10q+r)
 =10\left(5q+\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor\right)+5(r\bmod 2),
\]
and \(\lfloor r/2\rfloor<5\), formulas (1) and (5) imply
\[
D(5(10q+r))
 =D(5q)+\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor+5(r\bmod 2). \tag{6}
\]
Define the contribution of a last digit \(r\) after multiplication by \(5\) by
\[
h(r)=\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor+5(r\bmod 2),\qquad 0\le r<10.
\]
The crucial elementary identity is
\[
h(r)+h(9-r)=9. \tag{7}
\]
To see this without any exhaustive computation, split according to the parity of \(r\). If \(r=2t\), where \(0\le t\le4\), then
\[
h(r)=t,
\]
while \(9-r=2(4-t)+1\), and hence
\[
h(9-r)=(4-t)+5=9-t.
\]
If \(r=2t+1\), where again \(0\le t\le4\), then
\[
h(r)=t+5,
\]
while \(9-r=2(4-t)\), and hence
\[
h(9-r)=4-t.
\]
In either case their sum is \(9\), proving (7).

We next prove two complement identities. For every integer \(k\ge0\) and every \(x\) with \(0\le x<10^k\), let
\[
x^*=10^k-1-x
\]
be the \(k\)-digit decimal \(9\)-complement of \(x\), allowing leading zeros. We claim that
\[
D(x)+D(x^*)=9k, \tag{8}
\]
and also
\[
D(5x)+D(5x^*)=9k. \tag{9}
\]

We prove both identities by induction on \(k\).

For \(k=0\), the condition \(x<10^0=1\) forces \(x=0\), and then \(x^*=0\). Both sides of (8) and (9) are zero.

Suppose the identities are known for \(k\), and take \(x<10^{k+1}\). Write
\[
x=10q+r,
\qquad q=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{10}\right\rfloor,
\qquad r=x\bmod 10.
\]
Then \(q<10^k\) and \(0\le r<10\). If
\[
q^*=10^k-1-q,
\]
then direct subtraction gives
\[
10^{k+1}-1-x=10q^*+(9-r). \tag{10}
\]
Using (1), (10), and the induction hypothesis (8), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(x)+D(10^{k+1}-1-x)
 &=\bigl(D(q)+r\bigr)+\bigl(D(q^*)+9-r\bigr)\\
 &=9k+9\\
 &=9(k+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (8) at level \(k+1\).

For the multiplied identity, formula (6) says
\[
D(5x)=D(5q)+h(r).
\]
Applying the same formula to (10) gives
\[
D\bigl(5(10^{k+1}-1-x)\bigr)=D(5q^*)+h(9-r).
\]
Therefore, by the induction hypothesis (9) and the local identity (7),
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(5x)+D\bigl(5(10^{k+1}-1-x)\bigr)
 &=D(5q)+D(5q^*)+h(r)+h(9-r)\\
 &=9k+9\\
 &=9(k+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (9) and completes the simultaneous induction.

The two complement identities imply antisymmetry of the increments \(\varepsilon\). Fix \(k\ge0\), take \(x<10^k\), and set \(x^*=10^k-1-x\). By (8) and (9),
\[
D(5x)+D(5x^*)=D(x)+D(x^*).
\]
Rearranging in the integers yields
\[
D(5x^*)-D(x^*)=-\bigl(D(5x)-D(x)\bigr).
\]
Since \(\operatorname{sign}(-z)=-\operatorname{sign}(z)\) for every integer \(z\), including \(z=0\), we conclude that
\[
\varepsilon(10^k-1-x)=-\varepsilon(x)
\qquad(0\le x<10^k). \tag{11}
\]

We now apply this antisymmetry around the center in the conjecture. Fix \(k>0\), and abbreviate
\[
N=10^k,
\qquad
m=\frac N2-1.
\]
Because \(k>0\), \(N\) is even and at least \(10\). If \(t=N/2\), then \(m=t-1\) and \(N=2t\).

For \(0\le i\le m\), define the integer sum
\[
S_i=\sum_{j=m-i+1}^{m+i}\varepsilon(j), \tag{12}
\]
where a sum with lower endpoint larger than the upper endpoint is empty. Thus \(S_0=0\).

We claim that
\[
S_i=0\qquad(0\le i\le m). \tag{13}
\]
This follows by induction on \(i\). The base case has just been noted. Suppose \(i+1\le m\) and \(S_i=0\). Passing from \(S_i\) to \(S_{i+1}\) adds precisely one term at each end:
\[
S_{i+1}=\varepsilon(m-i)+S_i+\varepsilon(m+i+1). \tag{14}
\]
Put \(x=m-i\). This is a nonnegative integer less than \(N\), and its \(N-1\) complement is
\[
\begin{aligned}
N-1-x
 &=2t-1-(t-1-i)\\
 &=t+i\\
 &=m+i+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence (11) gives
\[
\varepsilon(m+i+1)=-\varepsilon(m-i).
\]
The two new endpoint terms in (14) therefore cancel, and \(S_{i+1}=S_i=0\). This proves (13).

Finally, let \(0\le i\le m\), and set
\[
L=m-i,
\qquad R=m+i.
\]
The difference between the two cumulative integer sums is exactly the intervening sum:
\[
F(R)-F(L)=\sum_{j=L+1}^{R}\varepsilon(j)
 =\sum_{j=m-i+1}^{m+i}\varepsilon(j)
 =S_i=0.
\]
Thus
\[
F(m-i)=F(m+i).
\]
Since \(a(n)\) is obtained from this cumulative sum by the same natural-number conversion at each index, equality of the integer sums implies
\[
a(m-i)=a(m+i).
\]
Recalling that \(m=10^k/2-1\), this is exactly
\[
a(m_k-i)=a(m_k+i)
\qquad	ext{for every }k>0	ext{ and every }0\le i\le m_k.
\]
This proves the conjectured symmetry.
